LESSON 63 OF 106·Web and Application Security Basics

Injection: SQL, Command and Template

What injection really is — data reinterpreted as instructions by a SQL, shell or template interpreter — and why parameterised queries remove the confusion instead of filtering around it.

Foundation15 min
Why this matters

Injection is what happens when data is treated as code. It is still one of the most damaging classes of web flaw because it turns data access into code execution, and it is usually a direct consequence of building queries with string concatenation.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • A query is code; a value inside it is data. Concatenating a value into the query moves it from data into code.
  • SQL injection lets an attacker change the meaning of a query, which can mean reading data they should not, changing data they should not, or in some configurations running commands on the server.
  • Command injection is the same idea against a shell: an argument containing shell metacharacters becomes a command.
  • Template and expression injection is the same idea again, applied to whatever a templating engine evaluates.
  • The fix in every case is the same in principle: keep data in a place the interpreter will never treat as instructions.

The background

  • Early web applications built queries by pasting request values into SQL strings, because there was no easier way.
  • Parameterised queries, called prepared statements, were available early but were not the default in most languages or drivers.
  • Object-relational mappers made query building convenient and accidentally reintroduced raw-string escaping as a fallback.
  • Cloud infrastructure as a service removed the easy shell escape, and pushed attackers toward reading data instead.

Real-world examples

  • A login form built by concatenating the username into a query can be bypassed without knowing any password.
  • A report feature that shells out to render a file can be turned into arbitrary command execution.
  • A templating engine evaluating user-supplied expressions turns a template preview into remote code execution.

What to look for

  • Check whether queries use parameter binding, or whether values are escaped into a string before the query runs.
  • Check whether a value can influence a table name, column name or sort order, since parameters cannot bind those.
  • Check for any call that passes user input to a shell, an evaluator or a template engine.
  • Check whether an ORM raw-query escape hatch is used anywhere near request data.

Key takeaways

  • Use parameterised queries or prepared statements for every value, and never build SQL by concatenation.
  • Map any dynamic identifier from a fixed allow-list rather than accepting it from the request.
  • Avoid invoking a shell; use library calls that take an argument array instead of a command string.
  • Keep templating engines out of paths where users can supply the template or the expression.
  • Run the database account with the least privilege it needs, so an injection cannot read or change more than it should.
